title: Wooruskhouse (Probable Copiague Neck)
summary: Rev. Azariah Horton repeatedly mentioned Wooruskhouse in 1741-1743 and located it about three miles from West Neck. The distance, his south-shore travel, the Town of Babylon's historic neck sequence, and the name's possible reference to a point of land make Copiague Neck the strongest modern inference, but not a proven identification.
address_label: Copiague Neck, Town of Babylon, NY (probable broad identification)
map_geometry_source: Probable Copiague Neck representative point inferred from Horton's approximately three-mile distance from West Neck, the historic west-to-east Babylon neck sequence, and modern mapped peninsula geography.
why_this_matters: Wooruskhouse records an eighteenth-century Native community landscape along Babylon's south shore. A probable marker restores that name to the map while making the limits of the surviving evidence visible instead of turning Horton's distance note into false certainty.
introduction_content: Wooruskhouse survives through the journal of missionary Azariah Horton. Tooker reported a consistent spelling and a distance of three miles from West Neck, now the westernmost neck in Amityville, but did not preserve a compass direction.
history_content: The Town of Babylon historian maps a west-to-east sequence of eleven south-shore necks beginning with West Neck in Amityville. Copiague Neck lies near the three-mile eastward distance indicated by Horton and remains a mapped peninsula today. This supports a probable landscape identification rather than an exact settlement point.
translation_content: Tooker cautiously compared Wooruskhouse with a term for a point or end of land. The comparison fits the neck landscape, but the derivation and the Copiague Neck identification both remain provisional.
preservation_content: This draft keeps the placename and Horton journal context available for review before any public map placement is added.
whereintheworld_content: The marker is a representative point on Copiague Neck. It reflects the strongest match among the mapped Babylon necks, not a recovered house, village center, or surveyed historic boundary.
